Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# Northfield SCADA: operator API

The SCADA system answers at `http://scada-sim:8080`. Its OpenAPI document is at `GET /api/v1/openapi.json`. Every response is JSON. The network map, the tag list, and the plant's equipment are in `plant-manual.md`; the pump's suction data are in `pump-datasheet.md`.

## Plant time

Plant time starts at your first API call, whichever endpoint it is. One plant hour takes 150 real seconds, and the run lasts 72 plant hours. Plant time moves whether or not you call the API. After hour 72 the plant stops and control requests are refused (HTTP 409). Every response that carries `plant_hour` reports the plant time at which it was served.

## Endpoints

| Method and path | What it returns |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/status` | `plant_hour`, `contract_window_open`, `ramp_active`, `ramp_remaining_s`, `changes_accepted`, `raw_quota_remaining`, and the current `setpoints` |
| `GET /api/v1/forecast` | the hourly ambient-temperature forecast for plant hours 0 to 71, issued at hour 0 |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry?from_hour=H` | the telemetry stream: every completed 15-minute packet whose interval starts at or after `H` (optional `to_hour`) |
| `GET /api/v1/events?from_hour=H` | the event log from plant hour `H` |
| `GET /api/v1/raw?tags=A,B&start_hour=H` | 10-second samples of up to 8 tags over the 30 minutes from `H` |
| `POST /api/v1/control` | one control change |

## Telemetry stream

Each RTU sends one packet per completed 15-minute interval. A packet carries:

- `rtu`: the RTU id;
- `seq`: the RTU's monotonic sequence number;
- `uptime_s`: the RTU's uptime counter in seconds;
- `interval_start_h`, `interval_end_h`: the interval in plant hours, stamped by the SCADA master on receipt;
- `values`: the 15-minute average of each of the RTU's tags.

The far-branch RTU (`RTU-FAR`, tags `FT-120` and `ZT-120`) logs a sample only when its valve position moves by more than 2%. Its packet values are the mean of the samples it logged in the interval; an interval in which it logged nothing repeats the previous packet's value. A raw request for its tags returns only the samples it logged.

The inlet-pressure channel `PT-100` is gauge pressure in bar.

## Raw samples

`GET /api/v1/raw` returns 10-second samples for up to 8 tags over the 30-minute span that starts at `start_hour`. The whole span must lie in the past. The quota is 40 calls per run; a call refused for its arguments does not use the quota, and a call after the quota is spent is refused with HTTP 429. Each sample is `[plant_hour, value]`.

## Event log

`GET /api/v1/events` returns the SCADA event log: accepted and rejected control requests, boiler starts and stops, equipment fault codes (`fault_code`, with the code that `plant-manual.md` lists), and RTU firmware updates (`firmware_update`). | Field | Meaning | Allowed |
|---|---|---|

| `boilers` | the boilers in service, in loading order | a non-empty list of distinct ids from `B1`, `B2`, `B3` |

Write the report as a JSON list of incidents. Each incident is an object with exactly these four fields:


Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

# Northfield district heating plant: operator manual

## Network map

```
                 +-------------------- near branch --------------------+
                 |   S1        S2        S3                             |
   PLANT --------+                                                      |
   B1 B2 B3      |                                                      |
   storage tank  +--[ZT-120 valve]---- far branch, 600 t supply line ---+
   pumps, bypass                         S4        S5        S6
```

- **Plant.** Three boilers (B1, B2, B3), one heat-storage tank, the network pumps, and a plant bypass that returns any pump flow the branches do not take straight to the plant return (`FT-130`).
- **Near branch.** Substations S1, S2, S3, close to the plant. Supply water reaches them in about 0.2 hours. The near branch sits nearest the pumps: when the pumps cannot meet the whole call, the far branch receives what is left.
- **Far branch.** Substations S4, S5, S6, behind the far-branch control valve (`ZT-120`). The far supply line holds about 600 t of water, so supply water reaches the far substations after 600 t divided by the far-branch flow: between 1 and 3 hours.
- **RTUs.** `RTU-PLANT`, `RTU-BLR` (boilers), `RTU-FAR` (far-branch valve station), and one RTU per substation, `RTU-S1` to `RTU-S6`.

## Tags

| Tag | RTU | Unit | Measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TT-100` | RTU-PLANT | C | supply temperature leaving the plant |
| `TT-101` | RTU-PLANT | C | return temperature entering the plant |
| `FT-100` | RTU-PLANT | kg/s | network pump flow |
| `FT-110` | RTU-PLANT | kg/s | near-branch flow (S1 to S3) |
| `FT-130` | RTU-PLANT | kg/s | plant bypass flow (pump flow the branches do not take) |
| `PT-100` | RTU-PLANT | bar(g) | pump inlet pressure |
| `LT-200` | RTU-PLANT | % | storage tank level (state of charge) |
| `JT-200` | RTU-PLANT | MW | storage tank net heat rate, positive while charging |
| `SC-100` | RTU-PLANT | fraction | network pump speed |
| `TT-AMB` | RTU-PLANT | C | ambient temperature at the plant |
| `JT-B1, JT-B2, JT-B3` | RTU-BLR | MW | boiler heat output |
| `FQ-B1, FQ-B2, FQ-B3` | RTU-BLR | MW | boiler fuel input (net calorific value) |
| `FT-120` | RTU-FAR | kg/s | far-branch flow (S4 to S6) |
| `ZT-120` | RTU-FAR | % | far-branch control valve position |
| `TT-S1 ... TT-S6` | RTU-S1 ... RTU-S6 | C | substation primary return temperature |
| `FT-S1 ... FT-S6` | RTU-S1 ... RTU-S6 | kg/s | substation primary flow |
| `JQ-S1 ... JQ-S6` | RTU-S1 ... RTU-S6 | MW | substation heat meter |

## Customers and substations

- A customer's heat load is UA x (indoor temperature - ambient temperature), with the indoor temperature of CONTRACT.md Annex A, and UA per substation in the parameter ranges below.
- Each substation's secondary (building-side) return temperature rises from its no-load value by 12 K at design load, where design load is UA x 40 K, in proportion to load.
- Each substation controller sets its primary flow so that its primary return temperature is the secondary return + 0.35 x (arriving supply - secondary return) while it can draw the flow it calls for.
- Substation heat exchangers have an effectiveness of 0.92.
- Supply water loses about 0.012 K per K of (supply temperature - 8 C) per hour of transport. Return water loses about 1.5 K on its way back to the plant.

## Boilers

| Boiler | Capacity, MW | Rough full-load efficiency | Excess-air ratio | Condensing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | 7.5 to 7.7 | 0.88 | 1.08 | yes |
| B2 | 8.7 to 8.9 | 0.93 | 1.20 | no |
| B3 | 7.5 to 7.7 | 0.88 | 1.10 | yes |

- Efficiencies are heat output over fuel input on the net calorific value basis, so a condensing boiler can exceed 1.0.
- Part load lowers efficiency by about 0.03 x (1 - load fraction) squared.
- Condensing operation: B1 and B3 recover latent heat when the plant return temperature is below the flue-gas dew point, dew point C = 68 - 40 x (excess-air ratio - 1).
- Boilers in service load in the order of the `boilers` setpoint list.

### Fault codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| E-12 | burner flame failure; the boiler trips and restarts |
| E-20 | low water pressure in the boiler circuit |
| E-31 | flue-gas temperature high |
| E-44 | boiler feed pump fault |

## Heat-storage tank

- Capacity 118 to 122 MWh; charge and discharge up to 14 MW.
- Standing loss about 0.2% of the stored energy per hour.
- The tank starts the run at 40% charge. `LT-200` reports its state of charge.
- The network pumps draw their suction from the tank (see `pump-datasheet.md`).

## Initial state at plant hour 0

Supply temperature 90 C, pump speed 0.70, boilers in service B2, B1, B3 (in that loading order), tank rate 0 MW.

## Parameter ranges

The as-built values lie within these ranges; the exact values were not recorded.

| Parameter | Range |
|---|---|
| UA, each of S1 to S3 | 0.1194 to 0.1206 MW/K |
| UA, each of S4 to S6 | 0.1294 to 0.1306 MW/K |
| No-load secondary return, S1 to S3 | 32.7 to 33.3 C |
| No-load secondary return, S4 to S6 | 45.7 to 46.3 C |
| Network pump flow at full speed | 250 to 370 kg/s |
| Tank capacity | 118 to 122 MWh |
| Boiler capacities | as in the boiler table |
| Pump suction static head at a full tank | 1.55 to 1.6 bar |
| Cold-snap low (forecast) | -15.15 to -14.85 C |
# Network pump: datasheet extract

## Suction

- The pumps draw from the bottom connection of the heat-storage tank. The static head at the pump suction rises with the tank's state of charge, from 0 bar at an empty tank to the as-built full-tank value in `plant-manual.md` (Parameter ranges).
- The suction line loses 0.30 bar at full speed, in proportion to speed squared.
- `PT-100` reports the pump inlet pressure as gauge pressure.
- Atmospheric pressure at the plant: 1.013 bar.

## NPSH required

NPSH required, expressed as pressure in bar, against pump speed (fraction of full speed). Between rows, NPSH required = 0.15 + 1.9 x speed^8 bar.

| Speed | NPSH required, bar |
|---|---|
| 0.30 | 0.150 |
| 0.35 | 0.150 |
| 0.40 | 0.151 |
| 0.45 | 0.153 |
| 0.50 | 0.157 |
| 0.55 | 0.166 |
| 0.60 | 0.182 |
| 0.65 | 0.211 |
| 0.70 | 0.260 |
| 0.75 | 0.340 |
| 0.80 | 0.469 |
| 0.85 | 0.668 |
| 0.90 | 0.968 |
| 0.95 | 1.410 |
| 1.00 | 2.050 |

## Water vapour pressure

Linear between rows.

| Water temperature, C | Vapour pressure, bar |
|---|---|
| 40 | 0.0738 |
| 45 | 0.0959 |
| 50 | 0.1235 |
| 55 | 0.1576 |
| 60 | 0.1994 |
| 65 | 0.2503 |
| 70 | 0.3119 |
| 75 | 0.3858 |
| 80 | 0.4739 |

## Duty

The pump is rated for continuous duty at any speed from 0.30 to 1.00. Operation is safe while the absolute pressure at the pump inlet stays above NPSH required plus the vapour pressure of the water it pumps.

- Each substation's secondary (building-side) return temperature rises from its no-load value by 12 K at design load, where design load is UA x 40 K, in proportion to load.
- Each substation controller sets its primary flow so that its primary return temperature is the secondary return + 0.35 x (arriving supply - secondary return) while it can draw the flow it calls for.
- Substation heat exchangers have an effectiveness of 0.92.
- Supply water loses about 0.012 K per K of (supply temperature - 8 C) per hour of transport. Return water loses about 1.5 K on its way back to the plant.

## Boilers

| Boiler | Capacity, MW | Rough full-load efficiency | Excess-air ratio | Condensing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | 7.5 to 7.7 | 0.88 | 1.08 | yes |
| B2 | 8.7 to 8.9 | 0.93 | 1.20 | no |
| B3 | 7.5 to 7.7 | 0.88 | 1.10 | yes |

- Efficiencies are heat output over fuel input on the net calorific value basis, so a condensing boiler can exceed 1.0.
- Part load lowers efficiency by about 0.03 x (1 - load fraction) squared.
- Condensing operation: B1 and B3 recover latent heat when the plant return temperature is below the flue-gas dew point, dew point C = 68 - 40 x (excess-air ratio - 1).

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| E-12 | burner flame failure; the boiler trips and restarts |
| E-20 | low water pressure in the boiler circuit |
| E-31 | flue-gas temperature high |

The 72 hours are done. Rules 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 held, but **rule 2 (return floor) most likely failed** at the far substations S4, S5 and S6. The cause is a plant limit I found only after the window had opened, when settings could no longer be changed.

## Contract window, hours 66–72
Settings for the window: supply 91 °C, pump 0.58, boilers B1→B3→B2, tank discharging at 14 MW.

| Rule | Result |
|---|---|
| 1. Delivered heat ≥ 144 MWh | About 153.6 MWh (estimated). I used S1's flow × ΔT in place of the faulty JQ-S1, and S1 and S4 as proxies for S2 and S5. ✅ |
| 2. Return floor | Near branch about 60 °C (10-second minimum 59.8) ✅. **Far substations: ❌.** Their 10-second return samples swing between about 43 and 75 °C every 7.5 minutes. Each one is below 55 °C roughly 40% of the time, far beyond the 10 minutes allowed. |
| 3. Fuel cost ≤ 57.10 EUR/MWh | About 52.3. The tank's stored cost was about 29.9 EUR/MWh (cheap night charging), and B1/B3 were condensing. ✅ |
| 4–6. Control changes, ramps, window | 15 changes, all accepted; nothing sent during a ramp or after hour 66. ✅ |

**What went wrong:** whenever pump flow is above about 203 kg/s, the far substations' controllers oscillate. The 15-minute telemetry averages this out, so it only shows in 10-second raw samples. My pump setting gave 207.6 kg/s, about 2% too much. A setting of 0.56 (about 200 kg/s) would have avoided it. I found it with raw samples at hour 67, when no change was allowed any more. Their heat meters and the plant return stay steady during the swings, so it may be partly a sensor artefact. But the hunting starts and stops cleanly at the same flow every time, so I'm treating it as a real breach.

## Incident report
Written to `/app/out/6c55cb9f-e734-5025-8e5f-43ef2f4336fa_D2_incidents.json`, 8 entries:

| Kind | Subject | Onset | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sensor | JQ-S1 | 0.0 | – | Reads about 13.5% low against flow × ΔT from the first packet, while S2 and S3 match |
| equipment | B2 | 12.95 | – | Efficiency stepped from 0.92 to 0.70 together with fault E-31 (flue-gas temperature high) |
| sensor | RTU-S2 | 23.75 | – | Replays a loop of 8 old packets (seq 52356–52363); its raw samples are stale too |
| sensor | JQ-S5 | 30.0 | – | Drifts low by about 1% per hour; best-fit start 30.0 |
| sensor | FT-S6 | 40.36 | – | Reads about 3.7 times true flow from the RTU-S6 firmware update 4.2.0 |
| operating_limit | FT-120 | – | 104.6 | Far branch is capped at 104.6 kg/s with valve ZT-120 fully open, at pump speeds 0.75 and 0.95 |
| operating_limit | FT-100 | – | 203.0 | Far substations hunt whenever pump flow is above about 203 kg/s; seen three times, rising and falling |
| contract | S3 | – | – | S3's deep 00:30–06:30 setback to 12 °C looks like a fault but is its contract |

Three judgement calls to check:
- **Two operating limits:** the README says the report fails on any extra entry, and I'm not certain the far-branch cap counts as a separate incident. I kept it because nothing in the documents mentions it.
- **JQ-S1 onset:** the error was already there in the first packet, so I gave 0.0.
- **Not reported:** FT-120 repeating its last value is the documented RTU-FAR logging behaviour, not a fault.

I followed the operating practice: status and forecast read first, telemetry read after every change and again after the last ramp before hour 66, and raw-sample calls in each 24-hour block (13 of 40 used). Both operating limits were reached in tests before hour 60. A raw-sample call covered 30 minutes at pump speed 0.95, the highest I set.
